points.pattern: Vます-form ／ い-adj ／ な-adj ＋ そうです
points.explain: This reports how something looks to you at the moment you speak. On a ます-stem it predicts an event that the present state seems to be leading up to, and words like 今{いま}にも, もうすぐ and これから often say when you expect it; on an adjective it offers a judgement about a quality you have not actually confirmed, as in 'this dish looks spicy'. Keep it well apart from the そうです of hearsay that arrives in Lesson 47: that one follows the plain form and passes on what you were told (雨{あめ}が 降{ふ}るそうです, 'I hear it will rain'), while this one follows the ます-stem and reports your own eyes (雨{あめ}が 降{ふ}りそうです, 'it looks like rain'). Note that いい becomes よさそうです and ない becomes なさそうです, and that adjectives of feeling such as うれしい need そうです when you describe somebody else, since you can only guess at how another person feels.
points.formation: Vます-form ／ い-adj（～い）／ な-adj［な］＋ そうです　（いい → よさそうです、ない → なさそうです）
examples: 今{いま}にも 雨{あめ}が 降{ふ}りそうです。
It looks like it will rain at any moment.
もうすぐ 桜{さくら}が 咲{さ}きそうです。
The cherry blossoms look as if they will be out soon.
この 料理{りょうり}は 辛{から}そうです。
ミラーさんは うれしそうです。
drills: It looks like it will rain at any moment.
今{いま}にも 雨{あめ}が 降{ふ}りそうです。
ます-stem ＋ そうです for something about to happen
The petrol looks as if it is going to run out.
ガソリンが なくなりそうです。
This dish looks spicy, doesn't it?
この 料理{りょうり}は 辛{から}そうですね。
an い-adjective drops its final い
This desk looks strong and durable.
この 机{つくえ}は 丈夫{じょうぶ}そうです。
a な-adjective drops な
Mr Miller looked happy today.
きょう ミラーさんは うれしそうでした。
with feelings, そうです is how you describe someone else
This dictionary looks good, so I'll buy it.
この 辞書{じしょ}は よさそうですから、買{か}います。
いい becomes よさそう

points.explain: A て-form plus 来{き}ます describes a round trip: you go somewhere, do the thing there, and come back to where you started, which is why it is what you call over your shoulder on the way out of the house or the office. The place takes で, because that is where the action happens, but it takes から when the point is fetching something away from there. Two set phrases follow the same shape — N（place）へ 行{い}って 来{き}ます when you do not name the action, and 出{で}かけて 来{き}ます when you name neither the place nor the action. Used with a verb of change such as なります, the same ending instead describes a change that has been coming on and has now reached the present: だんだん 寒{さむ}く なって 来{き}ました。
points.formation: ［V-て form］＋ 来{き}ます　（place で ／ から）　／　N(place)へ 行{い}って 来{き}ます　／　出{で}かけて 来{き}ます
examples: ちょっと たばこを 買{か}って 来{き}ます。
I'm just popping out to buy some cigarettes.
スーパーで 牛乳{ぎゅうにゅう}を 買{か}って 来{き}ます。
I'm going to the supermarket to buy some milk.
台所{だいどころ}から コップを 取{と}って 来{き}ます。
I'm going to fetch a glass from the kitchen.
郵便局{ゆうびんきょく}へ 行{い}って 来{き}ます。
I'm going to the post office and coming straight back.
drills: I'm just popping out to buy some cigarettes.
ちょっと たばこを 買{か}って 来{き}ます。
you are coming back, so 来{き}ます
I'm going to the supermarket to buy some milk.
スーパーで 牛乳{ぎゅうにゅう}を 買{か}って 来{き}ます。
the place of the action takes で
I'm going to fetch a glass from the kitchen.
台所{だいどころ}から コップを 取{と}って 来{き}ます。
から when you bring the thing away
I'm going to the post office and coming straight back.
郵便局{ゆうびんきょく}へ 行{い}って 来{き}ます。
used when you don't say what you will do there
I'm going out for a bit.
ちょっと 出{で}かけて 来{き}ます。
neither the place nor the action is named
It has gradually got colder.
だんだん 寒{さむ}く なって 来{き}ました。
with なります it marks a change that has reached the present
